questions.prompt: A 24 V DC relay coil has a resistance of 600 Ω. How much current does it draw, in milliamps?
questions.explanation: Ohm's law: I = V / R = 24 V / 600 Ω = 0.04 A, which is 40 mA.

questions.prompt: A 24 V DC power supply feeds loads that draw 2.5 A in total. How much power is it delivering, in watts?
The two wires to a limit switch touch each other where the insulation has worn through, so the switch is bypassed. What does its PLC input read?
options: TRUE all the time, whatever the switch does
FALSE all the time, whatever the switch does
It still follows the switch
The input card turns itself off
questions.explanation: The wires touching are a short across the switch: the input always has voltage, so it reads TRUE. A broken wire (an open) would read FALSE.

questions.prompt: A 300 Ω and a 900 Ω resistor are in **series** across 24 V DC. What is the voltage across the 900 Ω resistor, in volts?
questions.explanation: Total R = 300 Ω + 900 Ω = 1200 Ω, so I = 24 V / 1200 Ω = 0.02 A. Across the 900 Ω: 0.02 A × 900 Ω = 18 V (and 6 V across the 300 Ω; 18 V + 6 V = 24 V).

questions.prompt: Two Start buttons, A and B, are wired in **parallel** to a lamp. Fill in when the lamp is lit (TRUE = pressed, or lit).
questions.explanation: In parallel either button gives the current a path, so the lamp is lit when A or B (or both) is pressed.

questions.prompt: Six pilot lights are wired in **parallel** across 24 V DC. One lamp burns out (it opens). What happens to the other five?
options: They stay lit: each has its own path
They all go out
They get brighter, because they share its voltage
They flicker
questions.explanation: Each parallel branch has its own path and the full 24 V, so one opening leaves the others working. In series they would all go out.

questions.prompt: Match each part of a control panel to the power that comes out of it.

pairs.right: 480 V AC three-phase for the motors
120 V AC for coils and lights
24 V DC for PLC I/O and sensors

questions.explanation: The disconnect brings in the building's three-phase power; the control transformer steps it down to 120 V AC; the DC supply turns 120 V AC into 24 V DC.

questions.prompt: A PLC input card is labeled **24 V DC**. A technician wants to wire a 120 V AC button circuit to it. What is right?
options: Don't: a 24 V DC input card must not be wired to 120 V AC; it can be destroyed
It is fine: the card will read it as TRUE
It is fine if the button is normally closed
It is fine at 60 Hz but not at 50 Hz
questions.explanation: I/O cards are made for one kind of power. Read the label before wiring: 120 V AC on a 24 V DC input can destroy it.

questions.prompt: You have opened the disconnect, put your lock and tag on it, and bled the air pressure. What comes next, before you start work?
options: Verify zero energy: try the Start with everyone clear, and test for voltage with a meter, live-dead-live
Press the emergency stop to be sure
Start work: the lock makes it safe
Hand the key to the operator
questions.explanation: The last step of lockout/tagout is to verify zero energy. Only then is it safe to work. You keep your own key.

questions.prompt: Which of these keep a machine safe to work on? Choose every one that does.
options: Your own lock on the disconnect, with your own key
The emergency stop pressed in
The PLC program stopped
Stored energy released or blocked, and zero energy verified
questions.explanation: An e-stop and a stopped program are controls, not isolation: the machine can still be started and the panel is still live. Lockout with your own lock, stored energy released, and zero energy verified make it safe.
